summary: Redefines how the ECN field in the IP header is handled when entering and leaving an IP-in-IP tunnel. It updates RFC 3168 and RFC 4301 so that tunnels in IPv4 and IPv6 behave consistently, with new behaviors on exit.

eli5.summary: Congestion warning flags on packets could be lost when packets travel inside a tunnel. This sets clear rules for copying the flag in and out.

questions: how does ecn work in ip-in-ip tunnels
what is ecn normal mode and compatibility mode
what happens to not-ect packets with ce in the outer header
subtitle: How the two congestion bits in an IP header should be copied into and out of IP-in-IP tunnels.

tldr.problem: ECN lets routers mark packets instead of dropping them, but only the outer IP header is marked. The tunnelling rules in RFC 3168 and RFC 4301 disagreed with each other and could not carry more than one severity level of congestion.
tldr.mechanism: On entry, the tunnel ingress copies the ECN field into the outer header (normal mode), or clears it for old egresses (compatibility mode). On exit, the egress combines inner and outer fields using one table: it forwards the more severe marking, and drops a Not-ECT packet that arrives with CE on the outside.
tldr.outcome: All IP-in-IP tunnels behave the same way, two severity levels of congestion can pass through a tunnel, and the rules stay backward compatible because only previously unused combinations changed.

facts.label: Severity ranking
facts.value: CE, ECT(1), ECT(0), Not-ECT (high to low)

today: RFC 6040 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 9601. It has not been obsoleted, and it updates RFC 3168, RFC 4301 and RFC 4774.

sections.title: The Problem with ECN in Tunnels
sections.content:
Explicit congestion notification (ECN) lets a router tell endpoints that congestion is starting without dropping packets. It marks a proportion of packets in a two-bit ECN field in the IP header. A router marks only the outermost IP header it can see, so when a tunnel egress removes the outer header, it must combine the inner and outer ECN fields into one outgoing header.

The earlier rules grew apart. RFC 3168 blocked a two-bit covert channel by not copying CE into the outer header at the ingress. The IPsec architecture in RFC 4301 considered a two-bit covert channel a manageable risk and copied the whole field. At the egress, both still restricted how much of the field was passed on.

The trigger for this RFC was pre-congestion notification (PCN), which needs the ECN field copied at the ingress and needs four congestion states propagated at the egress. Existing tunnels propagated only three. The RFC covers only wire processing at tunnel endpoints, for IPv4 and IPv6, IPsec and non-IPsec, and makes no change to how congestion is marked or how senders respond.
sections.eli5: Warning flags on packets could get lost when packets travel inside a tunnel, and different tunnels handled them differently. This RFC makes them all follow one set of rules.

sections.title: ECN Codepoints and Terms
sections.content:
The ECN field has four codepoints: 00 Not-ECT (not ECN-capable transport), 01 ECT(1) and 10 ECT(0) (both ECN-capable), and 11 CE (congestion experienced).

The RFC names the tunnel endpoints. The encapsulator (ingress) adds an outer IP header, and the decapsulator (egress) removes it. The header being wrapped is the incoming header before encapsulation, then the inner header inside the tunnel. After removal, the egress builds the outgoing header by combining inner and outer fields.

Three actions on encapsulation are defined. Copying sets the outer ECN field equal to the incoming one. Zeroing sets it to Not-ECT. Resetting copies it except that CE becomes ECT(0).
sections.eli5: There are four kinds of stamp: no stamp allowed, two kinds of OK stamp, and a red warning stamp. The tunnel has an entrance and an exit, and it must decide which stamps to copy at each.

sections.title: What the Older RFCs Did
sections.content:
At the ingress, RFC 3168 full functionality mode reset a CE marking to ECT(0) in the outer header. RFC 4301 simply copied the field. RFC 3168 also had a limited functionality mode that set the outer header to Not-ECT, so packets in the tunnel were dropped rather than marked. That was needed to work with legacy decapsulators (RFC 2481, RFC 2401, RFC 2003) that would throw away outer markings.

At the egress, the rule was: if the inner field is Not-ECT, ignore the outer. Otherwise, if the outer is CE, the output is CE, and if not, the inner value is used. RFC 3168 added that a Not-ECT inner with a CE outer must be dropped, while RFC 4301 did not drop it.

This is why the old rules could not carry a distinction between ECT(1) and ECT(0): the outer ECT codepoints were ignored on exit.
sections.eli5: Some tunnels copied the stamp onto the envelope and some did not. Some tunnels threw away stamps added on the envelope, and some did not. It was a mess.

sections.title: Ingress: Normal and Compatibility Modes
sections.content:
An encapsulator always forwards the inner header without changing its ECN field. For the outer header it has two modes. In normal mode, which is REQUIRED, it MUST copy the two-bit ECN field of the incoming header. In compatibility mode it clears the outer field to Not-ECT. These are modes of the ingress only, not of the whole tunnel.

An ingress that may be paired with a legacy egress (RFC 2003, RFC 2401, RFC 2481 or the limited functionality mode of RFC 3168) MUST also implement compatibility mode. An IPsec ingress under RFC 4301 only needs normal mode, because IKEv2 key exchange ensures both ends comply with RFC 4301.

While discovering an egress, an ingress MUST send packets in compatibility mode. It can switch to normal mode if the egress indicates compliance. An ingress that claims compliance MUST NOT permanently disable ECN across the tunnel, and if it knows the egress propagates ECN, it SHOULD use normal mode.
sections.eli5: When the exit of the tunnel understands the stamps, the entrance copies them onto the envelope. When the exit is old and might not understand, the entrance leaves the envelope blank.

sections.title: Egress: One Decapsulation Rule
sections.content:
The decapsulator needs only one mode. It sets the outgoing ECN field from the table of inner and outer values. If the inner field is Not-ECT, it MUST NOT propagate any other codepoint: with a CE outer it MUST drop the packet, and with any other outer it MUST forward the packet as Not-ECT. In all other cases it MUST use the more severe marking of the two, ranked from highest to lowest as CE, ECT(1), ECT(0), Not-ECT.

Some combinations cannot result from any current or earlier ECN tunnelling specification. These currently unused combinations are marked in the table, and the decapsulator SHOULD log them and MAY raise an alarm. Alarms SHOULD be rate-limited, and it MUST be possible to suppress alarms or logging.

Because ECT(1) can rank above ECT(0), the rules let a scheme use ECT(1) as a more severe marking than ECT(0), which is what a two-level PCN encoding needs. A compliant egress also agrees to any mode request from a legacy ingress, since it behaves identically in all cases.
sections.eli5: When the envelope is opened, look at the stamps on the letter and the envelope and keep the worse warning. If the letter said no stamps were allowed but the envelope has a red warning, throw the letter away.

sections.title: Updates and Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
An RFC 4301 IPsec ingress is not changed at all, because normal mode is identical to its existing behaviour. An RFC 4301 egress and an RFC 3168 egress must adopt the new table. For RFC 3168 the change is that the outer is propagated when it is ECT(1) and the inner is ECT(0). For RFC 4301 there is also the new drop of Not-ECT inner with CE outer. Only combinations that have never been used changed.

An RFC 3168 ingress changes more: its full functionality mode reset CE, while normal mode copies it. The RFC calls this black-box backward compatible. Packets leaving the egress are identical, and only someone watching inside the tunnel sees CE markings that were not visible before.

A compliant endpoint is backward compatible with endpoints following RFC 4301, RFC 3168, RFC 2481, RFC 2401 or RFC 2003. Operators who want two congestion severity levels can require that their tunnels comply, and others can adopt the rules during normal code maintenance.
sections.eli5: Old tunnels keep working with new ones, because the new rules only fill in cases that never happened before. Someone has to look inside the tunnel to notice any difference.

sections.title: Security Trade-offs and Alternate Semantics
sections.content:
The rules trade information security (covert channels) against traffic security (congestion monitoring and control). Because IPsec cannot protect a mutable field like ECN, copying it at the ingress lets an inside sender signal a man in the middle, and copying it at the egress lets the man in the middle signal the receiver. The RFC accepts the bandwidth of a two-bit covert channel as manageable, and notes that allowing congestion notification to be lost would make enforcing congestion response harder.

It lists a few corner cases. Tunnels crossing the boundary of a Diffserv region with alternate ECN semantics could leak those semantics in or out. ECN nonce coverage is improved but still not perfect. A legacy ingress can ask the egress to turn off ECN, and the compliant egress agrees but still processes any ECN codepoints it actually receives, so the covert channel is not switched off.

Section 7 gives informative guidance for anyone designing alternate tunnelling semantics: avoid it if at all possible, clear the outer field unless the egress is known to propagate it, copy congestion to the outer header when it is, and define a behaviour for every combination of inner and outer headers.
sections.eli5: Copying warning stamps lets people pass tiny secret signals, but the authors decided that is a small enough risk. It is worth it so that congestion warnings are never lost.
